A new (and optimal) result for boundedness of solution of a quasilinear chemotaxis–haptotaxis model (with logistic source)

Ling Liu Affiliation:  Department of Basic ScienceJilin Jianzhu University, Changchun 130118, P.R.China    Jiashan Zheng ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail address: zhengjiashan2008@163.com (J. Zheng) Affiliation:  School of Mathematics and Statistics ScienceLudong University, Yantai 264025, P.R.China    Yu Li Affiliation:  School of Mathematics and Statistics ScienceLudong University, Yantai 264025, P.R.China    Weifang Yan Affiliation:  School of Mathematics and Statistics ScienceLudong University, Yantai 264025, P.R.China
Abstract

This article deals with an initial-boundary value problem for the coupled chemotaxis-haptotaxis system with nonlinear diffusion

{ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−χ∇⋅(u∇v)−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,τvt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−vw,x∈Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{w_{t}=-vw},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \end{array}\right. (0.1)

under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions in a smooth bounded domain Ω⊂ℝN​(N≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}(N\geq 1), where τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\} and χ\chi, ξ\xi and μ\mu are given nonnegative parameters. The diffusivity D⁡(u)D(u) is assumed to satisfy

D⁡(u)≥CD​(u+1)m−1​for all​u≥0​and​CD>0.D(u)\geq C_{D}(u+1)^{m-1}~\mbox{for all}~u\geq 0~~\mbox{and}~~C_{D}>0.

In the present work it is shown that if

m≥2−2N​λ​with​0<μ<κ0,m\geq 2-\frac{2}{N}\lambda~~\mbox{with}~~0<\mu<\kappa_{0},\begin{array}[]{ll}\\ \end{array}
m>2−2N​λ​with​μ≥κ0,m>2-\frac{2}{N}\lambda~~\mbox{with}~~\mu\geq\kappa_{0},\begin{array}[]{ll}\\ \end{array}

or

m>2−2N​and​μ=0m>2-\frac{2}{N}~~\mbox{and}~~~\mu=0

or

m=2−2N​and​CD>CG​N​(1+‖u0‖L1​(Ω))34​(2−2N)2​κ0,m=2-\frac{2}{N}~~\mbox{and}~~~C_{D}>\frac{C_{GN}(1+\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)})^{3}}{4}(2-\frac{2}{N})^{2}\kappa_{0},

then for all reasonably regular initial data, a corresponding initial-boundary value problem for (0.1)(0.1) possesses a unique global classical solution that is uniformly bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty), where

λ=κ0(κ0−μ)+\lambda=\frac{\kappa_{0}}{(\kappa_{0}-\mu)_{+}}

and

κ0={maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))​τ=1,χif​τ=0.\kappa_{0}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})~~\tau=1,\\ \chi~~~~~~\mbox{if}~~\tau=0.\\ \end{array}\right.

Here CG​NC_{GN} and λ0\lambda_{0} are the constants which are corresponding to the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality (see Lemma 2.1) and the maximal Sobolev regularity (see Lemma 2.2), respectively. Relying on a new LpL^{p}-estimate techniques to raise the a priori estimate of a solution from L1​(Ω)→Lλ−ε​(Ω)→Lλ​(Ω)→Lλ+ε​(Ω)→Lp​(Ω)​(for all​p>1)L^{1}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda-\varepsilon}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda+\varepsilon}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{p}(\Omega)(\mbox{for all}~p>1), these results thereby significantly extending results of previous results of several authors (see Remarks 1.1 and 1.2) and some optimal results are obtained.

Key words: Boundedness; Chemotaxis–haptotaxis; Nonlinear diffusion; Global existence

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification:  92C17, 35K55, 35K59, 35K20

1 Introduction

In order to describe the cancer cell invasion into surrounding healthy tissue, in 2005, Chaplain and Lolas ([4]) proposed a pioneering mathematical model which is called chemotaxis–haptotaxis model

{ut=∇⋅(D∇u)−χ∇⋅(u∇v)−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,τvt=Δv+u−v,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−vw,x∈Ω,t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u-v},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{w_{t}=-vw},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \end{array}\right. (1.1)

where DD, χ,ξ\chi,\xi and μ\mu are the cancer cell random motility, the chemotactic coefficients, the haptotactic coefficients and the proliferation rate of the cells, respectively. Here τ∈{0,1},\tau\in\{0,1\}, Ω⊂ℝN​(N≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}(N\geq 1) is the physical domain which we assume to be bounded with smooth boundary, and the unknown quantities uu, vv and ww represent the density of cancer cells, the concentration of matrix degrading enzymes (MDE) and the density of extracellular matrix (ECM), respectively.

As a subsystem, (1.1) contains the celebrated Keller–Segel ([17]) chemotaxis system (with logistic source, μ≠0\mu\neq 0)

{ut=∇⋅(D∇u)−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+μu(1−u),x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v+u−v,x∈Ω,t>0\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu u(1-u),\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u-v},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0\\ \end{array}\right. (1.2)

by setting w≡0w\equiv 0. Over the last four decades, there is a wide variety of patterns associated Keller–Segel system (1.2) have been studied extensively, and the main interest lies in whether the solution is global or blow up (see e.g., Cieślak [6], Cieślak and Winkler [5], Ishida et al. [13], Painter and Hillen [27], Winkler [47, 51, 51, 49], Li and Xiang [19], Tello and Winkler [42], Wang et al. [44], Zheng et al. [61]). In fact, if μ=0,\mu=0, the two behaviors (boundedness and blow-up) of solutions strongly depend on the space dimension and the total mass of cells ([2, 10, 11, 48]). When τ=0\tau=0, Tello and Winkler ([42]) mainly proved that the global boundedness for model (1.1) exists under the condition μ>(N−2)+N​χ\mu>\frac{(N-2)^{+}}{N}\chi, moreover, they gave the weak solutions for arbitrary small μ>0\mu>0. Kang and Stevens [16] (see also [53, 12]) improve the results of Tello and Winkler ([42]) to the case μ≥(𝐍−𝟐)+𝐍​χ\mu\geq{\bf\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi}. While if τ=1\tau=1 and μ>(N−2)+N​χ​CN2+11N2+1\mu>\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi C_{\frac{N}{2}+1}^{\frac{1}{\frac{N}{2}+1}} (where CN2+1C_{\frac{N}{2}+1} is a positive constant), Zheng ([61]) proved that for any sufficiently smooth initial data, the corresponding initial-boundary value problem for (1.2) possesses a globally defined bounded solution, which give the lower bound estimation for the logistic source, so that, improves the result of [47]. Furthermore, some recent studies have shown that the blow-up of solutions can be inhibited by the nonlinear diffusion (see Ishida et al. [13], Winkler et al. [1, 36, 55, 54, 46, 52]) and nonlinear logistic term (see [54, 56]).

There have been large literature on the global existence and the large time behavior of solutions to the system (1.1). We refer to [3, 22, 33, 37, 38, 41, 60] and the references therein. In fact, when τ=0\tau=0, MDEs diffuses much faster than cells (see [15, 38]), Tao and Wang [33] proved that model (1.1) possesses a unique global bounded classical solution for any μ>0\mu>0 in two space dimensions, and for large μ>0\mu>0 in three space dimensions. In [38],Tao and Winkler improved the condition on μ\mu (μ>(𝐍−𝟐)+𝐍​χ{\bf\mu>\frac{(N-2)^{+}}{N}\chi}), so that it coincides with the best one known for the parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system (1.2) (see Tello and Winkler[42]), moreover, in additional explicit smallness on w0w_{0}, they gave the exponential decay of ww in the large time limit. However, this problem is left open for the critical case μ=(𝐍−𝟐)+𝐍​χ{\bf\mu=\frac{(N-2)^{+}}{N}\chi}. While, if τ=1\tau=1, refined approaches involving a more subtle analysis of (1.1), Tao ([32]) and Cao ([3]) obtained the boundedness of global solution for the 2D and 3D space respectively, especially, for the 3D space, similar to the chemotaxis-only system ([61, 47]), the global solution is obtained only for large μ\mu, and it remains open for small μ\mu.

The diffusion of cancer cell may depend nonlinearly on their densities ([9, 30, 35]), and so we are led to consider the cell motility DD as a nonlinear function of the cancer cell density, D≡D⁡(u)=CD​(u+1)m−1,m∈ℝ,CD>0D\equiv D(u)=C_{D}(u+1)^{m-1},m\in\mathbb{R},C_{D}>0. Introducing this into the model (1.1) leads to the following chemotaxis-haptotaxis system with nonlinear diffusion

{ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−χ∇⋅(u∇v)−ξ∇⋅(u∇w)+μu(1−u−w),x∈Ω,t>0,τvt=Δv+u−v,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−vw,x∈Ω,t>0,D(u)∂u∂ν−χ∂v∂ν−ξ∂w∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),τv(x,0)=τv0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)-\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu u(1-u-w),\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u-v},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{w_{t}=-vw},\quad x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{D(u)\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-\chi\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}-\xi\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0},\quad x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)},\tau v(x,0)=\tau v_{0}(x),w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \end{array}\right. (1.3)

where u,vu,v and ww are denoted as before, μ≥0,τ∈{0,1}\mu\geq 0,\tau\in\{0,1\}, the diffusion function D⁡(u)D(u) fulfills

D∈C2​([0,∞))D\in C^{2}([0,\infty)) (1.4)

and there exist constants m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R} and CDC_{D} such that

D⁡(u)≥CD​(u+1)m−1​for all​u≥0.D(u)\geq C_{D}(u+1)^{m-1}~\mbox{for all}~u\geq 0. (1.5)

This parabolic-parabolic-ODE system (τ=1\tau=1 in (1.3)) and its parabolic-elliptic-ODE simplifications (τ=0\tau=0 in (1.3)) have been objects of extensive studies in recent decades. In fact, in N=2N=2, Zheng et al. ([62]) studied the global boundedness for model (1.3) with DD satisfies (1.4)–(1.5) and m>1m>1, moreover, in additional explicit smallness on w0w_{0}, they gave the exponential decay of ww in the large time limit. Moreover, if DD satisfies (1.4)–(1.5) with m>max⁡{1,m¯}m>\max\{1,\bar{m}\} and

m¯:={2​N2+4​N−4N⁡(N+4)​if​N≤8,2​N2+3​N+2−8​N​(N+1)N⁡(N+20)​if​N≥9,\bar{m}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{2N^{2}+4N-4}{N(N+4)}~~\mbox{if}~~N\leq 8,\\ \frac{2N^{2}+3N+2-\sqrt{8N(N+1)}}{N(N+20)}~~\mbox{if}~~N\geq 9,\\ \end{array}\right. (1.6)

Tao and Winkler ([35]) proved that model (1.3) possesses at least one nonnegative global classical solution, however, their boundedness is left as an open problem. Using the boundedness of ∫Ω|∇v|l​(1≤l<NN−1)\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{l}(1\leq l<\frac{N}{N-1}), Wang ([45]) and Li, Lankeit ([20]) proved that the global solvability and boundedness of classical solution (or weak solution) for any DD satisfies (1.4)–(1.5) and m>2−2Nm>2-\frac{2}{N}. Recently, Zheng ([58]) and Jin ([14]) extended these results to the case m>2​NN+2m>\frac{2N}{N+2} and m>0m>0 (as well as large μ\mu), respectively. But the cases m≤0m\leq 0 remain unknown. Other variants of the model that are commonly treated including the (nonlinear) logistic types and the re-establishment of ECM components, please refer to [29, 26, 39, 57], etc, and references therein. Thus it is meaningful to analyze the following question:

(Q)(Q): Which size of mm, χ,ξ\chi,\xi and μ\mu are sufficient to ensure boundedness of solutions to (1.3)?

It is our goal in this work to give answers to (Q)(Q). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result which gives a explicit condition between m,χ,ξm,\chi,\xi and μ\mu that yields to the boundedness of the solution.

Motivated by the above works, the aim of the present paper is to study the quasilinear parabolic–elliptic–ODE (τ=0\tau=0 in (1.3)) and parabolic–parabolic–ODE (τ=1\tau=1 in (1.3)) chemotaxis–haptotaxis model (1.3) under the conditions (1.4)–(1.5). Our main result is the following:

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝN​(N≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}(N\geq 1) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Assume that DD satisfy (1.4)–(1.5) and the initial data (u0,w0)(u_{0},w_{0}) fulfills

{u0∈C⁡(Ω¯)​with​u0≥0​in​Ω​and​u0≢0,w0∈C2+ϑ​(Ω¯)​with​w0≥0​in​Ω¯​and​∂w0∂ν=0​on​∂Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle{u_{0}\in C(\bar{\Omega})~~\mbox{with}~~u_{0}\geq 0~~\mbox{in}~~\Omega~~\mbox{and}~~u_{0}\not\equiv 0},\\ \displaystyle{w_{0}\in C^{2+\vartheta}(\bar{\Omega})~~\mbox{with}~~w_{0}\geq 0~~\mbox{in}~~\bar{\Omega}~~\mbox{and}~~\frac{\partial w_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0~~\mbox{on}~~\partial\Omega}\\ \end{array}\right. (1.7)

with some ϑ∈(0,1).\vartheta\in(0,1).

If one of the following cases holds:

(i)  m≥2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+m\geq 2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}} with 0<μ<χ0<\mu<\chi;

(ii)  m>2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+m>2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}} with μ≥χ\mu\geq\chi;

(iii)  m>2−2Nm>2-\frac{2}{N} with μ=0\mu=0;

(iv)  m=2−2Nm=2-\frac{2}{N} and CD>CG​N​(1+‖u0‖L1​(Ω))34​(2−2N)2​χC_{D}>\frac{C_{GN}(1+\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)})^{3}}{4}(2-\frac{2}{N})^{2}\chi;

then there exists a triple (u,v,w)∈(C0​(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞)))3(u,v,w)\in(C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,\infty)))^{3} which solves (1.3) in the classical sense. Here CG​NC_{GN} is a positive constant which is corresponding to the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality (see Lemma 2.1). Moreover, both uu, vv and ww are bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty).

Before we prove theorem 1.1, there exist a few remarks in order.

Remark 1.1.

(i) Theorem 1.1 extends the results of Theorem 1.1 of Tao and Winkler ([38]) for the critical case μ=(N−2)+N​χ\mu=\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi and D⁡(u)=1.D(u)=1.

(ii) If μ=0,\mu=0, in comparison to the result for the corresponding haptotaxis-free system ([52], w≡0w\equiv 0), it is easy to see that the restriction on mm here is optimal.

(iii) Observing that if μ≥(N−2)+N​χ\mu\geq\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi and w≡0w\equiv 0, then 2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+<12-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}}<1, therefore, Theorem 1.1 also extends the results of Theorem 1.1 of Tello and Winkler ([42]).

(iv) Obviously, if μ>χ\mu>\chi, then 2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+<12-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}}<1, so that, Theorem 1.1 extends the results of Theorem 1.1 of Tao and Winkler ([37]).

(v) Obviously, if w≡0w\equiv 0 and μ>0,\mu>0, then 2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+<2−2N2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}}<2-\frac{2}{N}, so that, Theorem 1.1 also partly extends the results of Theorem 1.1 of Wang et al. ([44]).

(vi) Obviously, if w≡0w\equiv 0, μ≥(N−2)+N​χ\mu\geq\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi and D⁡(u)≡1D(u)\equiv 1, then 2−2N​χ(χ−μ)+≤12-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\chi}{(\chi-\mu)_{+}}\leq 1, so that, Theorem 1.1 is consistent with the results of Theorem 3 of [16].

Theorem 1.2.

Let Ω⊂ℝN​(N≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}(N\geq 1) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Assume that DD satisfy (1.4)–(1.5) and the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) fulfills

{u0∈W1,∞​(Ω)​with​u0≥0​in​Ω​and​u0≢0,v0∈W1,∞​(Ω)​with​v0≥0​in​Ω​and​∂v0∂ν=0​on​∂Ω,w0∈C2+ϑ​(Ω¯)​with​w0≥0​in​Ω¯​and​∂w0∂ν=0​on​∂Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle{u_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)~~\mbox{with}~~u_{0}\geq 0~~\mbox{in}~~\Omega~~\mbox{and}~~u_{0}\not\equiv 0},\\ \displaystyle{v_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)~~\mbox{with}~~v_{0}\geq 0~~\mbox{in}~~\Omega~~\mbox{and}~~\frac{\partial v_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0~~\mbox{on}~~\partial\Omega},\\ \displaystyle{w_{0}\in C^{2+\vartheta}(\bar{\Omega})~~\mbox{with}~~w_{0}\geq 0~~\mbox{in}~~\bar{\Omega}~~\mbox{and}~~\frac{\partial w_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0~~\mbox{on}~~\partial\Omega}\\ \end{array}\right. (1.8)

with some ϑ∈(0,1).\vartheta\in(0,1). If one of the following cases holds:

(i)  m≥2−2N​maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+m\geq 2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}} with 0<μ<maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))0<\mu<\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)});

(ii)  m>2−2N​maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+m>2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}} with μ≥maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))\mu\geq\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)});

(iii)  m>2−2Nm>2-\frac{2}{N} with μ=0\mu=0;

(iv)  m=2−2Nm=2-\frac{2}{N} and CD>CG​N​(1+‖u0‖L1​(Ω))34​(2−2N)2​maxs≥1​λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))C_{D}>\frac{C_{GN}(1+\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)})^{3}}{4}(2-\frac{2}{N})^{2}\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)});

then there exists a pair (u,v,w)∈(C0​(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞))2𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸(u,v,w)\in(C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))^{2} which solves (1.3) in the classical sense, where CG​NC_{GN} and λ0:=λ0​(γ)\lambda_{0}:=\lambda_{0}(\gamma) are the constants which are corresponding to the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality (see Lemma 2.1) and the maximal Sobolev regularity (see Lemma 2.2), respectively. Moreover, both uu and vv are bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty).

Remark 1.2.

(i) Obviously, if μ>(N−2)+N​χ​maxs≥1​λ01s+1,\mu>\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}, 2−2N​maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+<12-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}}<1, hence, Theorem 1.2 extends the results of Ke and Zheng ([60]) and partly extends the result of Liu et al ([21]).

(ii) Obviously, if μ>0\mu>0, 2−2N​maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+<2−2N2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}}<2-\frac{2}{N}, hence Theorem 1.2 extends the results of Wang ([45]) and Li and Lankeit ([20]).

(iii) Theorem 1.2 extends the results of Zheng et al. ([59]) for the critical case μ≥(N−2)+N​χ\mu\geq\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi as well as w≡0w\equiv 0 and D⁡(u)=1.D(u)=1.

(iv) If μ=0\mu=0 and w≡0w\equiv 0, then (1.3) possess some solutions which blow up in finite time provided that DD satisfy (1.4)–(1.5) with m<2−2Nm<2-\frac{2}{N} (see e.g. [46, 6]). Therefore, In comparison to the result for the corresponding haptotaxis-free system (w≡0w\equiv 0 in (1.3)), it is easy to see that the restriction on mm here is optimal.

(v) If N=2N=2, then

2−2N​maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+=2−maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))[maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))−μ]+<1,2-\frac{2}{N}\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}}=2-\frac{\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})}{[\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})-\mu]_{+}}<1,

therefore, Theorem 1.1 extends the results of Wang et al. ([62]), who proved the possibility of global and bounded, in the cases, DD satisfies (1.4)–(1.5) with 𝐦>𝟏{\bf m>1}.

The main novelty and difficulty of the paper is how to control the chemotaxis term χ∇⋅(u∇v)\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v), haptotaxis term ξ∇⋅(u∇w)\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w) and strong degeneracies caused by system (1.3). To overcome this difficulty, the purpose of the present paper is to demonstrate how far an adequate combination of maximal Sobolev regularity theory and develop new LpL^{p}-estimate techniques (see Lemmas 3.4–3.11) can be used to obtain the global existence and boundedness of solutions to (1.3).

The rest of the paper is organized in the following way. Section 2 will be concerned with preliminaries, including some basic facts and a local existence result. In section 3, by careful analysis, this paper develops some LpL^{p}-estimate techniques to raise the a priori estimate of a solution from L1​(Ω)→Lλ−ε​(Ω)→Lλ​(Ω)→Lλ+ε​(Ω)→Lp​(Ω)​(for all​p>1)L^{1}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda-\varepsilon}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\lambda+\varepsilon}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{p}(\Omega)(~\mbox{for all}~~p>1), where

λ=κ0(κ0−μ)+\lambda=\frac{\kappa_{0}}{(\kappa_{0}-\mu)_{+}}

and

κ0={maxs≥1⁡λ01s+1​(χ+ξ​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω))​ifτ=1,χif​τ=0.\kappa_{0}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\max_{s\geq 1}\lambda_{0}^{\frac{1}{{{s}}+1}}(\chi+\xi\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})~~\mbox{if}~~~~\tau=1,\\ \chi~~~~~~\mbox{if}~~\tau=0.\\ \end{array}\right. (1.9)

To this end, by using the maximal Sobolev regularity and the standard estimate for the solution, we may derive entropy-like inequalities (see (3.26) and (3.23)). Then in order to estimate the right term ∫Ωuk+1\int_{\Omega}u^{k+1} and ∫Ωuk\int_{\Omega}u^{k} on the rightmost of (3.26) and (3.23), we need to deal with for two steps from ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lλ−ε​(Ω)→‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lλ​(Ω)\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\lambda-\varepsilon}(\Omega)}\rightarrow\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\lambda}(\Omega)} (see the proof of Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5), which plays a key rule in obtaining the main results. Then employing a bootstrap argument (see (3.48) and (3.49)), one could derive the boundedness of ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lλ+ε​(Ω)\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\lambda+\varepsilon}(\Omega)} (see Lemma 3.6). Relying on this, we develop new LpL^{p}-estimate techniques to raise the a priori estimate of solutions from Lλ+ε​(Ω)→Lp​(Ω)​(for all​p>1)L^{\lambda+\varepsilon}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{p}(\Omega)(\mbox{for all}~p>1) (see Lemmas 3.7–3.11). Finally, applying the standard Alikakos–Moser iteration, we prove the main results of this paper in the last part.

for some positive constant C4​(k)>0.C_{4}(k)>0. Substituting (3.46) into (3.44), we obatin that

and some positive constant C5C_{5}. Let k>λk>\lambda. Then by some basic calculation, we derive that

Lemma 3.7.

Assume that μ>0\mu>0. If

m≥2−2N​λ​with​μ<κ0,m\geq 2-\frac{2}{N}\lambda~~~\mbox{with}~~\mu<\kappa_{0},\begin{array}[]{ll}\\ \end{array} (3.52)

∫Ωuk​(x,t)​𝑑x≤C​for all​t∈(0,Tm​a​x),\int_{\Omega}u^{k}(x,t)dx\leq C~~~\mbox{for all}~~t\in(0,T_{max}), (3.53)

where λ\lambda and κ0\kappa_{0} are given by (3.42) and (1.9), respectively.

Proof.

Firstly, due to Lemma 3.6, we derive that there exists a positive constant C1C_{1} such that

4 The proof of main results

In this section, we are going to prove our main result. To this end, we will proceed in two steps. Firstly, applying the standard regularity theory of partial differential equation, we turn the bounds from Lemma 3.11 into a higher order bound for ∇v\nabla v.

Lemma 4.1.

Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 1.1 (or Theorem 1.2) hold. Let T∈(0,Tm​a​x)T\in(0,T_{max}) and (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be the solution of (1.3). Then there exists a constant C>0C>0 independent of TT such that the component vv of (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfies

‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞​(Ω)≤C​for all​t∈(0,T).\begin{array}[]{rl}\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C~~~\mbox{for all}~~t\in(0,T).\end{array} (4.1)
Proof.

Due to ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lp​(Ω)\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)} is bounded for any large pp (see Lemma 3.11), we infer from the standard regularity theory of parabolic equation (or elliptic equation, τ=0\tau=0) (see e.g. [7]) that (4.1) holds. ∎

The previous lemmas at hand, we can now pass to the proof of our main result. Its proof is based on a Moser-type iteration (see e.g. [36] and [18]).

Suppose on contrary that Tm​a​x<∞T_{max}<\infty. In view of (4.2), we apply Lemma 2.3 to reach a contradiction. Hence the classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (1.3) is global in time and bounded. ∎
